stem: A test started failing somewhere in the last 200 commits on `main`, and you know an old tag where it passed. What does `git bisect` do to find the commit that broke it?

options.text: It runs your tests on every commit in the range, newest first
options.why: That would be a linear search; bisect avoids testing every commit.

options.text: It binary-searches the range, checking out midpoints for you to judge
options.why: Each answer halves the remaining candidates, so ~200 commits need about 8 tests.

options.text: It compares the diffs of each commit and flags the one that touched the test
options.why: Bisect knows nothing about which files matter; it relies on your good/bad verdicts.

options.text: It reverts commits one at a time on a temporary branch until the test passes
options.why: Bisect never reverts anything; it checks out existing commits in a detached HEAD.

explanation: `git bisect start <bad> <good>` checks out a commit halfway between the two. You mark it `good` or `bad`, and Git halves the range again until one commit remains: "<sha> is the first bad commit". For n candidates that takes about log2(n) tests. Finish with `git bisect reset` to return to your branch.

stem: You add an executable `pre-commit` script to `.git/hooks/` in your repository and push. A teammate who then clones the repository gets the same hook and it runs on their commits.

options.text: True
options.why: Nothing under `.git/hooks/` is part of the repository content, so cloning never copies it.

options.text: False
options.why: Hooks live outside version control; a fresh clone only has the `.sample` files.

explanation: Hooks are local, per-clone files and are deliberately not transferred, because running code from a remote on checkout would be a security risk. To share hooks, commit them to a tracked folder and point `core.hooksPath` at it, or use a tool such as Husky, lefthook or the pre-commit framework. Each developer still has to opt in, which is why policy must also be enforced server-side or in CI.

stem: A repository includes another repository as a submodule at `libs/core`. What does the parent repository actually store for that path in each commit?

options.text: A full copy of the submodule files, refreshed on every commit
options.why: The parent never stores the submodule's files; that is what distinguishes a submodule from vendoring.

options.text: The name of the submodule branch to follow, such as `main`
options.why: An optional branch can be set in `.gitmodules`, but the tree records a commit, not a branch.

options.text: A pointer to one specific commit of the submodule (a gitlink)
options.why: The tree entry has mode 160000 and the submodule commit SHA, pinning an exact version.

options.text: A tarball of the submodule produced with `git archive` at commit time
options.why: Submodules are referenced by commit, not packaged into archives.

explanation: The superproject's tree contains a special "gitlink" entry (mode `160000`) holding the SHA of the submodule commit, and `.gitmodules` maps the path to a URL. Updating the submodule therefore means committing a new pointer in the parent repository.

stem: You are mid-way through a feature when an urgent bug needs fixing on `main`. You want a second checkout without stashing or cloning the repository again. Which command fits?

options.text: `git worktree add ../hotfix main`
options.why: It creates another working directory attached to the same repository and object store.

options.text: `git clone --shared . ../hotfix`
options.why: That makes a separate repository with its own refs; branches and commits aren't shared directly.

options.text: `git checkout --detach main` in the current folder
options.why: This switches your only working tree, which is what you wanted to avoid.

options.text: `git sparse-checkout set main`
options.why: Sparse checkout limits which paths appear; it doesn't create a second checkout.

explanation: `git worktree add <path> <branch>` creates a linked working tree with its own HEAD and index, sharing the object database and refs with the main repository. Commits made in either are immediately visible to the other, and `git worktree remove` cleans up when you are done.

stem: Roughly how many commits do you have to test with `git bisect` to find the first bad commit among 1,000 candidates? Type a number.
explanation: Bisect halves the candidate set each step, so it needs about log2(1000) ≈ 9.97, i.e. about 10 tests. Even 1,000,000 commits only need about 20. Skipped (untestable) commits can add a few extra steps.

stem: Match each client-side hook with when Git runs it.

options.text: Before the commit message is requested, after staging; a non-zero exit aborts the commit
After the message is written; receives the path of the message file
Before objects are sent to a remote during `git push`
After a successful `git checkout`/`git switch` updates the working tree

explanation: `pre-commit` runs first and is used for linters and tests. `commit-msg` gets the message file path as `$1` and can reject the message. `pre-push` receives the remote name and URL as arguments and the refs on stdin. `post-checkout` runs after the working tree is updated and cannot affect the outcome.

stem: A repository uses Git LFS for `*.png`. What is stored in the Git history for a tracked PNG?

options.text: A compressed copy of the PNG, with a smaller delta for each new version
options.why: That is how ordinary Git blobs work; LFS exists to avoid storing large binaries in history.

options.text: A small text pointer (SHA-256 and size); the bytes live in LFS storage
options.why: The real bytes are uploaded to LFS storage and swapped in by the smudge filter on checkout.

options.text: A symlink to a path on the shared network drive configured for LFS storage
options.why: LFS pointers aren't symlinks; they are plain text files the filter understands.

options.text: Nothing: tracked files are excluded from commits like ignored files
options.why: LFS files are committed, just as pointers rather than full content.

explanation: With `*.png filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text` in `.gitattributes`, the clean filter replaces each PNG with a ~130-byte pointer (`version`, `oid sha256:…`, `size …`) when you stage it. The binary is uploaded to the LFS store on push and downloaded on checkout, which keeps clones of the Git history small.

stem: Which two of these hooks run on the developer's machine rather than on the server that receives pushes? (Choose two.)

options.text: `pre-commit`
options.why: It runs in the local repository when you run `git commit`.

options.text: `pre-receive`
options.why: It runs on the remote while it processes a push, before any ref is updated.

options.text: `pre-push`
options.why: It runs locally during `git push`, before anything is sent.

options.text: `post-receive`
options.why: It runs on the server after refs are updated, often to trigger deployments.

options.text: `update`
options.why: It is a server-side hook run once per ref being pushed.

explanation: Client-side hooks (`pre-commit`, `commit-msg`, `pre-push`, `post-checkout`, …) run in the developer's clone and can be skipped or simply not installed. Server-side hooks (`pre-receive`, `update`, `post-receive`) run in the repository that accepts pushes, so they are where self-hosted servers enforce policy. Hosted services such as GitHub use branch protection and status checks instead.

stem: After `git clone https://example.com/app.git`, the `libs/core` directory exists but is empty, and `git submodule status` prints a line starting with `-`. What brings the submodule's files in?

options.text: `git pull --rebase` in the parent repository
options.why: Pulling updates the parent; it doesn't initialise uncloned submodules by default.

options.text: `git submodule update --init --recursive`
options.why: This registers the submodule, clones it and checks out the recorded commit, including nested ones.

options.text: `git checkout -- libs/core`
options.why: The parent only has a gitlink there, so there are no files to restore.

options.text: `git lfs pull`
options.why: LFS fetches large-file content; submodules are a separate mechanism.

explanation: A plain clone leaves submodules uninitialised: the directory exists, and `git submodule status` marks it with `-`. Run `git submodule update --init --recursive`, or clone with `--recurse-submodules` in the first place. Setting `submodule.recurse=true` makes later checkouts and pulls update submodules automatically.

stem: A teammate clones a repository on a new laptop and opens `assets/logo.png`. The image viewer fails, and the file turns out to be a 130-byte text file starting with `version https://git-lfs.github.com/spec/v1`. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The PNG was corrupted by line-ending conversion because `-text` is missing
options.why: Line-ending damage changes bytes in the real file; it doesn't replace it with an LFS pointer.

options.text: Git LFS isn't installed on that machine, so checkout wrote the pointer text
options.why: Without the LFS filter, checkout writes the pointer text itself; `git lfs install` then `git lfs pull` fixes it.

options.text: The file was too large for Git, so GitHub truncated it to its first 130 bytes
options.why: Hosts reject oversized pushes outright; they don't truncate files.

options.text: The repository is a shallow clone, so older file contents were not downloaded
options.why: Shallow clones still contain full content for the commits they include.

explanation: In history, an LFS-tracked file is a small pointer (`version`, `oid sha256:…`, `size …`); in a test repository, a 50,000-byte PNG became a 130-byte pointer. The `filter=lfs` smudge step downloads the real content during checkout, but only if Git LFS is installed and initialised. Otherwise the pointer text is written as the file.

stem: You set up a `pre-commit` hook in `.git/hooks/` that blocks commits containing `console.log`, and it works for you. A colleague still manages to commit `console.log` calls. They never used `--no-verify`. Why?

options.text: Hooks only run for the user who created them, based on file ownership
options.why: Git runs any executable hook in the repo; ownership isn't the issue here.

options.text: Their Git version ignores hooks written as shell scripts
options.why: All supported Git versions run executable hooks of any language.

options.text: Hooks in `.git/hooks/` aren't versioned, so their clone has no hook
options.why: Each clone has its own `.git/hooks/`; yours was never shared.

options.text: The hook only runs on the `main` branch unless configured otherwise
options.why: Hooks run for every commit; branch filtering would have to be in the script.

explanation: The `.git` directory isn't part of what is pushed, so your hook exists only in your clone. Commit the hooks to a tracked folder and have everyone run `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`, or use a hook manager installed by the project's setup script. Because client hooks can always be skipped, repeat important checks in CI.

stem: You automate a bisect with `git bisect run ./check.sh`. Some commits in the range don't compile, so the test can't say anything about them. How should `check.sh` report those commits?

options.text: Exit 1 so they are treated as bad and bisect moves on
options.why: Marking an unbuildable commit bad can make bisect blame the wrong commit.

options.text: Exit 125 so bisect skips them and picks a nearby commit
options.why: Exit code 125 means "can't test this one"; bisect then tries another candidate.

options.text: Exit 0 so they are treated as good and bisect moves on
options.why: Calling them good can hide the real first bad commit among them.

options.text: Exit 128 so bisect retries the same commit after a rebuild
options.why: Codes of 128 or more abort `git bisect run` instead of skipping.

explanation: `git bisect run` interprets the script's exit code: 0 = good, 1–127 except 125 = bad, 125 = skip, and anything ≥128 or negative aborts the run. Using 125 for "untestable" keeps broken builds from skewing the result; if the only remaining candidates are skipped, bisect lists all of them as possible culprits.

stem: Branch `hotfix` is already checked out in a linked worktree at `../wt-a`. In the main repository you run `git worktree add ../wt-b hotfix`. What happens?

options.text: A second checkout of `hotfix` is created, and commits in either one move the branch
options.why: Git refuses this to stop two working trees from fighting over one branch tip.

options.text: Git creates `../wt-b` on a new branch `hotfix-1` automatically
options.why: Git doesn't invent branch names; you'd pass `-b` yourself.

options.text: It fails: fatal: 'hotfix' is already used by worktree at '…/wt-a'
options.why: A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time.

options.text: Git moves `hotfix` out of `../wt-a`, leaving that worktree detached
options.why: Existing worktrees are never altered by adding another one.

explanation: Each branch may be checked out in at most one worktree. Use `git worktree add -b new-branch ../wt-b hotfix` to start a new branch from it, `--detach` for a detached checkout, or `--force` if you really want a second checkout. The same rule applies to `main` in the original working tree.

stem: Inside a `git bisect run` script, which exit code tells bisect to skip the current commit because it cannot be tested? Type the number.
explanation: Exit 125 marks the commit as untestable (equivalent to `git bisect skip`). Other codes from 1 to 127 mean bad, 0 means good, and a code of 128 or higher aborts the automated run.

stem: Put the steps of a manual bisect session in order.

options.text: `git bisect start`
`git bisect bad` on the current, broken commit
`git bisect good v2.3.0`, a release known to work
Test each commit Git checks out and mark it `good` or `bad`
`git bisect reset` once Git names the first bad commit

explanation: Start the session, mark one bad and one good commit, then repeat the test-and-mark loop on each midpoint Git checks out. When Git prints "… is the first bad commit", run `git bisect reset` to return to the branch you started from. (`git bisect start <bad> <good>` combines the first three steps.)

stem: You `cd libs/core`, commit a fix inside the submodule, then return to the parent repository. `git status --short` there prints ` M libs/core`. What does that mean?

options.text: Files in `libs/core` still have uncommitted edits that need `git add -p` first
options.why: The submodule's own changes are committed; the parent is reporting something else.

options.text: The submodule moved past the commit the parent records; commit the new pointer
options.why: Staging `libs/core` in the parent and committing updates the gitlink.

options.text: The `.gitmodules` file was modified and must be committed
options.why: That would show as `M .gitmodules`, not as the submodule path.

options.text: The submodule is detached and its commit will be garbage-collected
options.why: Being out of sync with the pointer doesn't schedule anything for deletion.

explanation: The parent tracks a specific submodule commit. After committing inside the submodule its HEAD moved, so the parent reports the path as modified; `git diff --submodule=log` shows which commits were added. Run `git add libs/core` and commit in the parent, and push the submodule commit too, otherwise others get a pointer to a commit they can't fetch.

stem: Your team wants every developer to run the same commit hooks. Which two approaches actually share hooks through the repository? (Choose two.)

options.text: Commit hooks to `.githooks/` and have each developer set `core.hooksPath` to it
options.why: The scripts are versioned; one config setting makes Git run them.

options.text: Commit the `.git/hooks/` directory like any other folder
options.why: Git won't track files inside `.git`; they can't be committed.

options.text: Use a hook manager such as Husky or the pre-commit framework, installed by the project's setup
options.why: They keep hook config in the repo and install it locally on setup.

options.text: Push with `git push --hooks` so the remote distributes them
options.why: No such option exists; Git never transfers hooks.

options.text: Add `hooks=shared` to `.gitattributes`
options.why: Attributes control per-path behaviour like diff or merge, not hooks.

explanation: Hooks are never cloned, so sharing them always needs a versioned copy plus a local opt-in step. Pointing `core.hooksPath` at a tracked folder is the built-in way; hook managers automate the same idea. Because a developer can skip either, critical rules also belong in CI or server-side checks.

stem: `git commit --no-verify` skips both the `pre-commit` and the `commit-msg` hooks.

options.text: True
options.why: `--no-verify` (`-n`) bypasses the pre-commit and commit-msg hooks.

options.text: False
options.why: It isn't limited to pre-commit; commit-msg is skipped too.

explanation: The `-n`/`--no-verify` option bypasses `pre-commit` and `commit-msg`. Other hooks such as `prepare-commit-msg` and `post-commit` still run. `git push --no-verify` similarly skips `pre-push`. Because these are client-side, anyone can bypass them, which is why enforcement belongs on the server or in CI.

stem: To ship new commits to an air-gapped server, you run `git bundle create update.bundle v1.4..main`. On the server, `git bundle verify update.bundle` fails with "Repository lacks these prerequisite commits". Why?

options.text: Bundles can only contain full histories, never ranges
options.why: Ranged (incremental) bundles are supported and common.

options.text: A ranged bundle needs its base commit, and this repository lacks `v1.4`
options.why: The bundle omits history before `v1.4` and lists it as a prerequisite.

options.text: Bundles are signed with the creator's key, which the server doesn't trust
options.why: Bundles aren't signed; verification only checks contents and prerequisites.

options.text: The server's Git uses SHA-256, and the bundle uses SHA-1
options.why: A hash-algorithm mismatch gives a different error.

explanation: A bundle built from `A..B` contains only the commits after `A`, and records `A` as a prerequisite. `git bundle verify` checks the receiving repository has those commits. Create a full bundle (for example `git bundle create repo.bundle --all`) the first time, then incremental ones based on what the receiver already has.

stem: You run `git bisect run ./t.sh` over commits c1 (good) to c16 (bad). The bug was actually introduced in c8, but `t.sh` exits 125 for c7 because it doesn't build. How does bisect end?

options.text: It names c8, because skipped commits are ignored once a neighbour is tested
options.why: Bisect can't rule out c7 without testing it, so it can't be sure about c8.

options.text: It names c7, because skipped commits are treated as bad by default
options.why: Skipped commits are untested, not bad.

options.text: It reports only skipped commits remain; the culprit is c7 or c8
options.why: With c6 good, c7 untestable and c8 bad, bisect can't decide between c7 and c8.

options.text: It aborts with an error because 125 is reserved for internal use
options.why: Exit 125 is the documented "skip" code, not an error.

explanation: When a skipped commit sits right next to the boundary, bisect stops with "There are only 'skip'ped commits left to test. The first 'bad' commit could be any of:" followed by the candidates (here c7 and c8). Make c7 testable, or inspect both commits by hand, to finish. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: A repository has an executable `.git/hooks/pre-commit` that always exits 1. You then run `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`; `.githooks/` contains only a `commit-msg` hook. What happens when you commit with a valid message?

options.text: The commit is blocked, because Git runs hooks from both directories
options.why: Git reads hooks from exactly one directory, not both.

options.text: It succeeds, because Git now reads hooks only from `.githooks/`
options.why: Setting `core.hooksPath` replaces `.git/hooks/` as the hook directory.

options.text: It fails with an error that `.githooks/pre-commit` is missing
options.why: A missing hook is simply not run; it isn't an error.

options.text: Git copies `.git/hooks/pre-commit` into `.githooks/` and runs it
options.why: Git never copies hooks between directories.

explanation: `core.hooksPath` changes where Git looks for every hook. Once set, hooks still sitting in `.git/hooks/` are ignored entirely; in a test, the always-failing `pre-commit` stopped running and only `.githooks/commit-msg` fired. Teams migrating to a shared hooks folder must move all the hooks they still want.

stem: You write a `pre-push` hook to block pushes that would update `refs/heads/main`. Where does the hook find out which refs are being pushed?

options.text: In an environment variable `GIT_PUSH_REFS`, as a comma-separated ref list
options.why: Git sets no such variable for pre-push.

options.text: As command-line arguments: one argument per ref being pushed
options.why: The arguments are only the remote name and URL.

options.text: On stdin, one line per ref: local ref, local SHA, remote ref, remote SHA
options.why: Read stdin in a loop and check the third field for `refs/heads/main`.

options.text: By running `git status` inside the hook to see the pending push
options.why: Status doesn't describe an in-progress push; the data comes on stdin.

explanation: Git calls `pre-push` with the remote name and URL as `$1` and `$2`, and writes one line per ref to stdin, for example `refs/heads/main <sha> refs/heads/main <sha>` (an all-zero remote SHA means a new ref). Exiting non-zero aborts the push before anything is sent. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: Your self-hosted Git server has a `pre-receive` hook that rejects direct pushes to `main`. A developer runs `git push --no-verify origin main`. What happens?

options.text: The push succeeds, because `--no-verify` disables all hooks for that push
options.why: `--no-verify` only skips the local `pre-push` hook.

options.text: It's rejected: the server's pre-receive hook declines the push
options.why: Server-side hooks run on the server, which the client can't switch off.

options.text: The push succeeds and the hook only logs a warning on the server
options.why: A non-zero exit from pre-receive rejects every ref in the push.

options.text: Git retries the push without hooks after the first rejection
options.why: Git never retries a rejected push on its own.

explanation: Client flags can't influence the receiving repository. The server ran its `pre-receive` hook, printed its stderr as `remote: …`, and declined the push with "pre-receive hook declined". That is why policy that must hold belongs in server-side hooks, or in branch protection on hosted services. Verified against a local bare repository.

stem: A monorepo contains `README.md`, `services/shared.js`, `services/api/a.js`, `services/web/w.js` and `docs/d.md`. You run `git sparse-checkout set services/api` (cone mode, the default). Which three files are present in your working tree afterwards? (Choose three.)

options.text: `README.md`
options.why: Cone mode always includes files at the repository root.

options.text: `services/shared.js`
options.why: Files directly inside parent directories of a cone are included.

options.text: `services/api/a.js`
options.why: This is the directory you asked for, so all of it is checked out.

options.text: `services/web/w.js`
options.why: Sibling directories of the selected one are excluded.

options.text: `docs/d.md`
options.why: Other top-level directories are excluded.

explanation: In cone mode, selecting a directory checks out that directory recursively, plus every file (not subdirectory) at the root and in each parent directory. A test with Git 2.55 left `README.md`, `services/shared.js` and `services/api/a.js`, while `ls-files -t` marked the others as skip-worktree (`S`). That behaviour is what makes cone patterns fast to match.

stem: A repository already has two years of `.psd` files committed normally and is 3 GB. You run `git lfs track "*.psd"` and commit `.gitattributes`. Fresh clones are still 3 GB. Why, and what actually shrinks them?

options.text: LFS needs a few days to migrate files in the background after tracking starts
options.why: LFS doesn't touch history on its own; nothing happens in the background.

options.text: Clones are cached by the host; ask the host to clear its cache
options.why: The size comes from the commits themselves, not a cache.

options.text: `track` only affects new commits; rewrite history with `git lfs migrate import`
options.why: Old commits still contain the full blobs until history is rewritten.

options.text: `.gitattributes` must be committed before the first `.psd` for LFS to take effect
options.why: Ordering in the new commit doesn't matter; the old commits are the problem.

explanation: Tracking a pattern changes how files are stored from then on; every existing commit still holds the real PSD blobs. `git lfs migrate import --include="*.psd" --everything` rewrites history to replace them with pointers. That changes commit SHAs, so it needs a force-push and a coordinated re-clone by everyone.

stem: You deleted a linked worktree's folder with `rm -rf ../wt-d` instead of `git worktree remove`. Now `git branch -d exp` fails with "cannot delete branch 'exp' used by worktree at '…/wt-d'". What fixes it?

options.text: Run `git worktree prune`, then delete the branch
options.why: Prune removes administrative entries for worktrees whose folder is gone.

options.text: Run `git gc --aggressive` so the deleted worktree's objects are cleaned up
options.why: Garbage collection doesn't clear worktree records; the branch would stay locked.

options.text: Recreate `../wt-d` with `mkdir` so Git can detect and close it
options.why: An empty directory isn't a valid worktree; the record would still be wrong.

options.text: Delete the branch with `git update-ref -d` because worktrees lock it permanently
options.why: Locks aren't permanent; prune is the supported way to clear them.

explanation: Git keeps per-worktree metadata under `.git/worktrees/<name>`. If the folder vanishes, `git worktree list --porcelain` marks it "prunable" and the branch still counts as checked out. `git worktree prune` (also run during `gc`) clears those records, after which `git branch -d exp` works. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: A CI script needs to know whether the working tree is dirty and which files changed. Which two outputs are safe for a script to parse or test? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git status --porcelain` (v1 or v2)
options.why: Porcelain formats are documented as stable and are not translated.

options.text: Plain `git status` text, matched against "nothing to commit"
options.why: Human output can change between versions and is localised.

options.text: The exit code of `git diff --quiet` (0 clean, 1 changed)
options.why: Exit codes are a stable interface and need no parsing.

options.text: `git branch` output with the `*` marker stripped
options.why: This is a porcelain command for people; prefer `for-each-ref` or `rev-parse`.

options.text: Colour codes in `git log --color` to spot merge commits
options.why: Formatting and colours aren't a machine contract.

explanation: For automation, use plumbing commands or porcelain output modes that Git promises to keep stable: `status --porcelain`, `for-each-ref --format`, `rev-parse`, and exit codes such as `diff --quiet` (verified: 0 when clean, 1 with unstaged changes). Human-oriented output can change wording, ordering or language between releases.

stem: In a shell script, `git diff --quiet` runs in a repository whose working tree has unstaged changes. What exit status does it return? Type the number.
explanation: `--quiet` suppresses output and implies `--exit-code`: 0 means no differences and 1 means differences were found. Scripts use it as `if ! git diff --quiet; then …`. `git diff --cached --quiet` checks staged changes in the same way.

stem: A release script runs `git archive -o release.tar HEAD`. The tarball contains `README.md` and `src/`, but not the `tests/` folder that is committed in the repository. What explains it?

options.text: `git archive` skips directories whose names start with `test` by convention
options.why: There is no such built-in convention.

options.text: `.gitattributes` marks `tests/ export-ignore`, so archive leaves it out
options.why: The `export-ignore` attribute removes paths from `git archive` output.

options.text: The folder is in `.gitignore`, which `git archive` honours
options.why: `.gitignore` only affects untracked files; a committed folder would be archived.

options.text: Archive only includes files changed since the last tag
options.why: It exports the whole tree of the given commit, not a diff.

explanation: `git archive` exports the tree of a commit, so untracked files are never included, and it honours the `export-ignore` attribute (and `export-subst` for keyword expansion). A test with `tests/ export-ignore` in `.gitattributes` produced a tar without `tests/`.

stem: After `git submodule update`, a developer `cd`s into `libs/core`, makes two commits and pushes the parent repository. A week later their submodule commits are gone from `git log` in `libs/core`. What went wrong?

options.text: Submodule commits are deleted whenever the parent is pushed
options.why: Pushing the parent never deletes commits in a submodule.

options.text: The submodule HEAD was detached, so the commits were left on no branch
options.why: Without a branch, the new commits became unreachable after HEAD moved away.

options.text: The parent's `.gitmodules` URL was wrong, so the commits went to another remote
options.why: A wrong URL affects fetching, not whether local commits stay reachable.

options.text: LFS was not installed, so the submodule's commits were stored as pointers
options.why: LFS deals with file content, not commits.

explanation: `git submodule update` checks out the recorded commit in detached-HEAD state. Commits made there belong to no branch; when the next update checks out another commit they become unreachable (recoverable only via the submodule's reflog until it expires). Create or switch to a branch inside the submodule before committing, push the submodule first, then commit and push the new pointer in the parent.

stem: Match each need in a very large monorepo to the Git feature that addresses it.

options.text: Partial clone, `--filter=blob:none`
Sparse checkout
Shallow clone, `--depth=1`
`git maintenance start`

prompts.text: Keep full commit history but download file contents only when they are needed
Only materialise the `services/api` directory in the working tree
A CI job that just builds the latest commit and needs no history
Keep the repository fast with scheduled background prefetch and repacking

explanation: Partial clone keeps all commits and trees but fetches blobs on demand, so history commands still work. Sparse checkout limits the working tree to chosen directories. Shallow clones truncate history, which is fine for one-off CI builds but breaks bisect and blame. `git maintenance start` registers scheduled tasks such as prefetch, commit-graph updates and incremental repacks.

stem: Put the steps for cleanly removing the submodule `libs/core` from a repository in order.

options.text: `git submodule deinit -f libs/core` to unregister it and empty the folder
`git rm libs/core` to remove the gitlink and its `.gitmodules` entry
Delete `.git/modules/libs/core` to drop the submodule's stored repository
Commit the change in the parent repository

explanation: `deinit` removes the submodule's section from `.git/config` and clears its working tree. `git rm` removes the gitlink and updates `.gitmodules`. Git keeps the submodule's own repository under `.git/modules/` in case you add it back, so delete it if you want it gone. Finally commit, so others pick up the removal.

stem: You attach a note with `git notes add -m "reviewed" HEAD` and then run `git push origin main`. The note is now on the remote.

options.text: True
options.why: Notes live under `refs/notes/`, which a branch push doesn't include.

options.text: False
options.why: You must push `refs/notes/*` explicitly, for example `git push origin refs/notes/*`.

explanation: Notes are stored as commits on `refs/notes/commits`, separate from branches, so pushing `main` doesn't send them; in a test, the remote had only `refs/heads/main` afterwards. Push and fetch the notes ref explicitly (or add a refspec) if the team should share them.

stem: `git bisect run ./test.sh` stops on its first step with "bisect run failed: exit code 137 … is < 0 or >= 128". The test runner was killed for using too much memory. What does this tell you about using test runners in `bisect run`?

options.text: Bisect treats any crash as "bad" and continues, so the result is still valid
options.why: Codes of 128 or more abort the run; nothing is marked.

options.text: Codes ≥128 abort the run; wrap the runner so crashes map to 1 or 125
options.why: A wrapper decides deliberately whether a crash means bad, skip or abort.

options.text: Bisect retries the commit up to three times before giving up
options.why: There is no retry logic in `bisect run`.

options.text: The script must print "good" or "bad"; exit codes are ignored
options.why: Bisect reads only the exit code, never the output.

explanation: `git bisect run` maps 0 → good, 125 → skip, 1–127 → bad, and treats ≥128 or negative codes as a fatal error. Processes killed by signals (137 = SIGKILL, 139 = SIGSEGV) therefore abort the session. A small wrapper script that normalises the runner's result keeps automated bisects reliable. Verified: a script exiting 200 aborts with this message.

stem: You create `git bundle create repo.bundle main` and clone it elsewhere with `git clone repo.bundle app`. The clone prints "warning: remote HEAD refers to nonexistent ref, unable to checkout" and the working tree is empty. What should the bundle have included?

options.text: The `--depth` option, because bundles default to shallow history
options.why: Bundles aren't shallow by default; the history arrived fine.

options.text: `HEAD` as well as `main` (or `--all`), so clone knows what to check out
options.why: Without a HEAD ref in the bundle, clone has nothing to check out.

options.text: A tag, because `git clone` only checks out tagged commits when reading bundles
options.why: Clones check out the bundle's HEAD, not tags.

options.text: The `.git/config` file, since bundles don't carry remotes
options.why: Remotes are irrelevant here; the missing piece is HEAD.

explanation: A bundle is a packfile plus the refs you list. If HEAD isn't listed, `git clone` can't decide what to check out; in a test it warned and left an unborn branch. `git bundle create repo.bundle HEAD main` (or `--all`) produced a clone that checked out normally. You could also run `git checkout main` in the clone afterwards.

stem: A `post-commit` hook in repository A runs `git -C ../B pull` to keep a sibling repository updated. Running the same command by hand works, but inside the hook it acts on repository A. What is the likely cause?

options.text: Hooks always run with the current directory set to `.git`, which overrides `-C`
options.why: `-C` changes the directory but doesn't override inherited repository variables.

options.text: Hooks inherit an exported `GIT_DIR`; unset it before targeting another repo
options.why: An inherited `GIT_DIR` makes nested Git commands target repository A.

options.text: Hooks run as a different user who can't read `../B`
options.why: The hook runs as the user who ran `git commit`.

options.text: `git pull` is disabled inside hooks to prevent loops
options.why: Git places no such restriction on commands inside hooks.

explanation: The githooks documentation notes that environment variables such as `GIT_DIR` and `GIT_WORK_TREE` are exported to hooks so that Git commands in the hook find the right repository. A command meant for a different repository inherits them too. Clear them first, for example `unset GIT_DIR GIT_WORK_TREE GIT_INDEX_FILE`, or run the command with `env -u GIT_DIR …`.

stem: Compliance requires every commit on `main` to reference a ticket ID like `ABC-123`, with no exceptions. Which two controls actually enforce this? (Choose two.)

options.text: A server-side `pre-receive` or `update` hook that rejects pushes containing bad messages
options.why: It runs on the server, so developers can't skip it.

options.text: A `commit-msg` hook committed to `.githooks/` with `core.hooksPath` set
options.why: It helps developers, but `--no-verify` or an unset config skips it.

options.text: A required CI status check on pull requests, with branch protection blocking direct pushes
options.why: Merges are blocked until the check passes on the server side.

options.text: A `prepare-commit-msg` hook that pre-fills the ticket ID
options.why: Pre-filling is a convenience; users can still delete or edit it.

options.text: A commit message template set with `commit.template`
options.why: Templates only suggest text; they enforce nothing.

explanation: Only controls that run where developers have no say can guarantee a rule. On self-hosted servers that is a server-side hook; on hosted platforms it is branch protection or rulesets plus a required status check. Client hooks are still worth having for fast feedback, but they are advisory.

stem: `main` is built from many merged feature branches, and individual commits inside those branches often don't build. You want bisect to identify which merge into `main` introduced a regression. Which option helps most?

options.text: `git bisect skip` on every feature-branch commit by hand
options.why: Workable but slow; there is a built-in way to restrict the walk.

options.text: `git bisect start --no-checkout` so commits aren't built or checked out
options.why: That avoids checking out files; it doesn't change which commits are visited.

options.text: `git bisect start --first-parent`, so it only walks merges on `main`
options.why: It follows first parents only, so you test integrated states of `main`.

options.text: Rebase all feature branches to make history linear before bisecting
options.why: Rewriting shared history is disruptive and unnecessary here.

explanation: By default bisect may check out commits from inside merged branches. `--first-parent` (Git 2.29+) follows only the first parent of merge commits, so each tested commit is a state that existed on `main`, and the culprit reported is the merge that brought the bug in. You can then bisect inside that feature branch if needed.

stem: Your `.gitmodules` sets `branch = main` for `libs/core`. What is the difference between `git submodule update` and `git submodule update --remote`?

options.text: They are identical; the `branch` setting makes both follow `main`
options.why: Plain update ignores the branch setting and uses the recorded commit.

options.text: Plain update uses the recorded commit; `--remote` checks out the branch tip
options.why: You still have to commit the new pointer in the parent.

options.text: `--remote` updates `.gitmodules` with the latest URL, while plain update leaves it alone
options.why: URL syncing is `git submodule sync`; `--remote` is about which commit.

options.text: Plain update pulls `main` into the submodule, while `--remote` pushes local submodule commits
options.why: Neither command pushes anything.

explanation: The parent's gitlink is the source of truth for plain `update`, which makes builds reproducible. `--remote` fetches the configured branch and checks out its latest commit; the parent then shows the submodule as modified, and you commit that new pointer deliberately. The branch setting only matters for `--remote`.

stem: You have the main working tree and two linked worktrees of one repository. Which three things does each worktree have its own copy of? (Choose three.)

options.text: `HEAD`
options.why: Each worktree checks out its own branch or commit.

options.text: The index (staging area)
options.why: Staging in one worktree doesn't affect another.

options.text: The working files on disk
options.why: Each worktree is a separate directory of checked-out files.

options.text: Branches under `refs/heads/`
options.why: Refs are shared: a commit on a branch in one worktree is visible in all.

options.text: The object database
options.why: All worktrees share one object store, which is why they are cheap.

explanation: A linked worktree's `.git` is a file pointing to `.git/worktrees/<name>` in the main repository, which holds its private HEAD, index and other per-worktree state. Objects, branches, tags and the stash stack live in the shared "common dir"; `git rev-parse --git-dir` and `--git-common-dir` show the split.

stem: A GitHub Actions job uses `actions/checkout@v4` with default settings. Tests that read `fixtures/model.bin` (tracked by Git LFS) fail because the file is a small text pointer. What is the fix?

options.text: Run `git lfs track "*.bin"` in the workflow before the tests
options.why: Tracking affects future commits; it doesn't download content.

options.text: Set `fetch-depth: 0` so the full history, including LFS objects, is fetched
options.why: Depth controls commits fetched; LFS content needs a separate download.

options.text: Set `lfs: true` on the checkout step (or run `git lfs pull` afterwards)
options.why: The checkout action skips LFS content by default.

options.text: Commit the `.bin` files without LFS so CI can read them
options.why: That defeats LFS and bloats history.

explanation: `actions/checkout` defaults to `lfs: false`, so LFS-tracked files arrive as pointers. Enabling `lfs: true` (or running `git lfs pull` after checkout) downloads the content. It counts against LFS bandwidth, so cache it if many jobs need it.
reference: GitHub actions/checkout README; Git LFS docs

stem: CI clones a huge repository and then runs `git blame` and `git bisect` on old code. Which clone option cuts the initial download while keeping those commands working?

options.text: `--depth=1`, because blame and bisect only ever need the most recent commit
options.why: Both need history; a depth-1 clone has none to walk.

options.text: `--filter=blob:none`: all commits, with file contents fetched on demand
options.why: History is complete, and file contents download lazily.

options.text: `--single-branch --no-tags`, which removes the need for old blobs
options.why: This trims refs but still downloads every blob on the branch.

options.text: `--bare`, since bare clones don't download file contents
options.why: A bare clone has no working tree but still includes all objects.

explanation: A blobless partial clone downloads every commit and tree but no file contents until they are needed. Commands that walk history work, fetching missing blobs as they go. Shallow clones cut history itself, which breaks bisect and blame beyond the depth. For very large repos, a treeless clone (`--filter=tree:0`) is even smaller but slower for history-heavy commands.

stem: `git ls-tree HEAD libs/core` prints `<mode> commit df99a08…	libs/core` for a submodule. What is the mode shown for this gitlink entry? Type the number.
explanation: Gitlinks use the special mode `160000` and object type `commit`, distinguishing them from regular files (`100644`), executables (`100755`), symlinks (`120000`) and subtrees (`040000`). Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: A teammate's commits show GitHub's "Verified" badge. You rebase their branch onto the latest `main` and push. The rebased commits no longer show "Verified". Why?

options.text: GitHub removes badges from any branch that was force-pushed
options.why: Badges reflect each commit's own signature, not how the branch was updated.

options.text: Rebasing makes new commits, which the old signatures can't cover
options.why: New commits are signed only if you sign them yourself, with your key.

options.text: Signatures expire after a fixed number of days and must be renewed
options.why: Commit signatures don't expire like that.

options.text: The teammate's key is only valid on their original branch name
options.why: Keys aren't tied to branch names.

explanation: A signature covers the exact commit object, including its parent. Rebasing rewrites commits with new parents and committers, so the originals' signatures can't apply. If `commit.gpgsign` is on, the new commits are signed by you; otherwise they are unsigned. Teams that require signed commits often prefer merge commits, or have each author rebase and re-sign their own work.
reference: GitHub Docs: About commit signature verification

stem: A deploy script must create branch `release/1.4` only if it doesn't exist yet. Which check is the most robust?

options.text: `git branch | grep -q "release/1.4"`
options.why: Grep also matches substrings like `release/1.40` and depends on human output.

options.text: `git checkout release/1.4 2>/dev/null || git checkout -b release/1.4`
options.why: Checkout can fail for other reasons, such as local changes, and then a new branch is wrongly attempted.

options.text: `git rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/heads/release/1.4`
options.why: It exits 0 with the SHA if the exact ref exists, and 1 with no output if not.

options.text: `git log -1 release/1.4 > /dev/null`
options.why: This also resolves tags or remote branches of that name, and errors are noisy.

explanation: Scripts should ask Git precise questions through plumbing. `rev-parse --verify --quiet` with a fully qualified ref name answers exactly "does this branch exist", via its exit status (verified: 1 and no output for a missing ref). `git show-ref --verify --quiet refs/heads/…` works the same way.
